metadata.note: Passenger rail at St. Joseph, Missouri. St. Joseph's Union Depot opened in 1896 at 1200 S. 6th Street and was worked by six roads - the Santa Fe, the Burlington Route, the Chicago Great Western, the Rock Island, the Missouri Pacific and the Union Pacific - several of them reaching the city on other companies' rails: the Missouri Pacific came in over the Burlington, the Chicago Great Western used Santa Fe trackage south of town and Burlington trackage north of it, and the Union Pacific reached Troy, Kansas over the Rock Island. Between 1959 and 1961 the surviving roads moved out of Union Depot to their own stations before quitting passenger service altogether: Union Pacific in 1952, the Rock Island and the Chicago Great Western in 1962, the Santa Fe in 1969 and the Burlington in 1971. Two electric interurbans also served the city, the St. Joseph and Savannah northward from 1910 and the Kansas City, Clay County and St. Joseph - the longest interurban out of Kansas City - from 1913. This layer covers the Burlington's Missouri River route through St. Joseph and both interurbans; see incomplete_coverage for what is not here and why.

metadata.incomplete_coverage: NOT YET ADDED, and the reason in each case. (1) The Hannibal and St. Joseph Railroad of 1859 - the first railroad across Missouri, the line that carried mail to the Pony Express - is the most important omission. A corridor-constrained trace was attempted over every OSM railway way within 3-4 km of the St. Joseph - Cameron - Chillicothe - Brookfield - Macon - Palmyra - Hannibal corridor: only 52 percent of the 302 km corridor has any mapped track within 3 km, and 64 percent within 4 km, with unmapped stretches of 58, 32, 24 and 18 km. OSM does carry ways named 'Hannibal and St. Joseph Railroad' (about 93 km of them) but they do not connect, and widening the tolerance far enough to bridge the holes puts the route on other companies' rails. Drawing it would mean inventing well over a third of the line, so it is left out rather than guessed at. (2) The St. Joseph and Grand Island (St. Joseph west across Kansas to Grand Island, Nebraska, the Union Pacific connection) - no OSM route relation found for the St. Joseph - Troy - Hiawatha portion. (3) Chicago Great Western north toward Des Moines - OSM has a 42 km chain of CGW-tagged abandoned way out of St. Joseph but not the through route. (4) Rock Island and (5) Santa Fe at St. Joseph - fragmentary CRI&P- and AT&SF-tagged ways only. (6) The Missouri Pacific never had its own line into St. Joseph, reaching it over Burlington trackage rights, so there is nothing separate to draw. (7) The city streetcar system of the St. Joseph Railway, Light, Heat and Power Company is not included; it began under animal power and would need its electrification date established before anything could be drawn, per the horsecar rule.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: The opening date of the Kansas City - St. Joseph half of the route: the Platte Country/Missouri Valley Railroad predecessors are not clearly dated in any source found, so that feature starts at the documented 1870 consolidation rather than at its real opening, which was earlier. Also unsourced: all headways here; the exact 1971 date on which the Burlington's last St. Joseph passenger train ran; and whether the 1900 CB&Q lease changed the operating crews or only the corporate control.

segments.note: The longest interurban running out of Kansas City, at nearly 60 miles. The St. Joseph line opened May 5 1913, four months after the company's Excelsior Springs line, and ran big wooden-and-steel cars close to 60 feet long that were reported to touch 70 mph. Improved roads and cheap automobiles killed it and regular service ended in 1933; frequency estimated, unsourced
